title: Google Cloud deployment and network boundaries
summary: An organization of projects, a Databricks account, two compute planes and one query path: who owns each boundary on Google Cloud, how a denied request differs from an unreachable one, and which capabilities stay unknown until verified.
outcomes: Place the Databricks account, the classic compute plane and a serverless workspace against an organization's folders and projects, and name every resource's owner.
Trace one query's author, control, execution and storage paths with a named identity and owning project at each hop.
Explain service accounts, bucket IAM, the customer-managed VPC, Cloud NAT, Private Google Access, firewall priority and Private Service Connect as separate boundaries.
Run ordered diagnoses for a denied and an unreachable request and assemble an evidence matrix that keeps unverified Google Cloud capabilities unknown.
startingAssumptions: The platform module separates account, workspace, catalog, compute and storage.
The cloud bridge and the trust-boundary lesson have covered DNS, routing, identity and authorization in general terms.
editorialRationale: Google Cloud deployment teaching fails when it relabels an AWS or Azure picture, so the module starts from Google's own organization, folder and project hierarchy, places each workspace and service account by owner, and follows one query with named identities. It then treats storage identity, the VPC's subnet and outbound paths, firewall priority and Private Service Connect as separate boundaries. Serverless connectivity is taught as an honest unknown because the sources read disagree, and the module closes with a separately sourced comparison with AWS and Azure, two ordered diagnoses and an evidence matrix the three-cloud lab reuses.

claims.description: A classic Databricks workspace on Google Cloud names, as its cloud resource container, the project it uses to instantiate the workspace's cloud resources, plus a region; its network configuration records the project that holds the VPC and subnet; by default Databricks creates a VPC in that project for each workspace, a customer-managed VPC is recommended and an existing workspace cannot be migrated to one; account-level APIs are called by account admins with Google-issued OIDC tokens at accounts.gcp.databricks.com.

claims.description: A serverless workspace on Google Cloud is created with compute mode SERVERLESS and a region and needs no prerequisite resources; Databricks' reference template gives it no project container and no network configuration; the account API's storage modes are CUSTOMER_HOSTED and DEFAULT_STORAGE; classic workspaces report the effective compute mode HYBRID.
claims.context: Databricks on Google Cloud serverless workspaces; availability by region and account must be verified.

claims.description: A Google service account is owned by the project named when it is created, which forms part of its email; the workspace service account has the form db-<workspace-id>@prod-gcp-<region>.iam.gserviceaccount.com; provisioning uses a customer service account added to the Databricks account console as an account admin and granted a custom Workspace Creator role; a cluster can carry a Google service account used for Cloud Storage and BigQuery; the service account with access to a customer-managed key exists within the Databricks control-plane project; a Compute Engine VM supports one attached service account whose tokens code on the VM reads through the metadata server.
claims.context: Identities in a Databricks on Google Cloud deployment; the default classic VM account is not settled by these sources.

claims.description: On Google Cloud a Unity Catalog storage credential creates a Databricks-managed service account whose email is granted access to buckets, and Databricks' Unity Catalog guide binds roles/storage.objectAdmin and roles/storage.legacyBucketReader on the bucket; an external location combines a gs:// path with a storage credential; with uniform bucket-level access only bucket-level or higher IAM policies control access; testIamPermissions reports the permissions the caller itself holds on a bucket.
claims.context: Unity Catalog storage access on Google Cloud; minimum roles must be read from the current Databricks page.

claims.description: A customer-managed VPC for a classic workspace on Google Cloud supplies a subnet in the workspace's region, with a netmask between /29 and /9, from whose range Compute Engine cluster nodes are allocated, and outbound access to the public network through Cloud NAT or a similar customer-managed appliance; one VPC can serve several workspaces but a subnet cannot be reused by other workspaces or resources; secondary pod and service ranges and the GKE configuration are deprecated and no longer supported.
claims.context: Classic compute networking on Google Cloud; firewall and Private Google Access requirements are not settled by these sources.

claims.description: Private Google Access lets VMs in a subnet reach Google services without external IP addresses; a Cloud NAT gateway lets VMs in the chosen subnets reach the internet without external IP addresses; a VM without an access configuration has no external internet access; Databricks' examples enable Private Google Access on the node subnet, and Databricks' reference template creates no Cloud Router or Cloud NAT when back-end Private Service Connect is used.
claims.context: Outbound paths from classic compute on Google Cloud.

claims.description: Google Cloud firewall rules allow or deny ingress or egress for instances in a VPC network; direction defaults to ingress; priority runs from 0 to 65535 with 1000 as default, lower numbers take precedence and a deny beats an allow at equal priority; implied rules sit at priority 65535; target tags or target service accounts narrow a rule, and without them it applies to every instance in the network; the Databricks Workspace Creator role includes permission to read and create firewall rules, and Databricks' reference template creates an ingress rule for the Databricks subnet before the workspace and, when hardened without PSC, an egress rule using the region's control-plane IP addresses.
claims.context: VPC firewall rules; the rules Databricks requires must be read from the current customer-managed VPC page.

claims.description: Back-end Private Service Connect for Databricks on Google Cloud uses two endpoints, one for the secure cluster connectivity relay and one for REST APIs; each is a forwarding rule in the customer's VPC whose target is a Databricks service attachment, registered in the Databricks account with its project, endpoint name and region and listed in the network configuration as dataplane_relay or rest_api; a workspace must be created with private access settings to support PSC scenarios; Databricks' reference template requires a customer-managed VPC and adds a private Cloud DNS zone for gcp.databricks.com, visible to the VPC, with records for the workspace URL, its dp- variant and tunnel.<region>.gcp.databricks.com; a PSC connection's status can be ACCEPTED, PENDING, REJECTED, CLOSED or NEEDS_ATTENTION.
claims.context: Classic private connectivity on Google Cloud; regional service attachments, tier and release status must be verified.

claims.description: A front-end PSC endpoint, placed in a transit VPC, carries user connections to the Databricks web application, REST API and Databricks Connect API; private access settings choose ACCOUNT level, which admits VPC endpoints registered in the Databricks account, or ENDPOINT level, which admits only listed endpoint IDs; public_access_enabled defaults to true on Google Cloud and false on AWS, and with public access enabled an IP access list restricts public sources; the API description allows disabling public access only with both front-end and back-end private connections.
claims.context: Front-end private connectivity and private access settings; the API description is partly worded for AWS.

claims.description: The Databricks Terraform provider documentation at v1.133.0 states that NCC binding is available for AWS and Azure only and in Public Preview on AWS, that NCC private endpoint rules are available on Azure and in Public Preview on AWS, and documents only AWS and Azure default and target rule types; the Databricks SDK for Python v0.141.0 models a gcp_endpoint on NCC private endpoint rules with a target service attachment, Google API hostnames or all APIs that support VPC Service Controls; network policies list GOOGLE_CLOUD_STORAGE as a storage destination type.
claims.context: Serverless connectivity on Google Cloud: the read sources conflict, so availability is unknown until verified.

claims.description: On AWS the Databricks network configuration takes at least two subnets in different availability zones with netmasks between /17 and /25 plus security groups, and a storage credential's IAM role requires a trust policy; Azure Databricks workspaces are Azure resources whose injected virtual network uses two subnets delegated to Microsoft.Databricks/workspaces with network security groups, with Private Link private endpoints for back-end, front-end and browser authentication, and storage credentials can use an Azure Databricks access connector's managed identity.
claims.context: Contrast only; the AWS and Azure modules own their clouds' answers.

claims.description: For a customer-managed key on Databricks on Google Cloud, the service account with access to the Cloud KMS key exists within the Databricks control-plane project, and with the manual option Databricks does not use OAuth to grant it access; Databricks' reference architecture applies keys to managed services (notebooks, secrets and Databricks SQL query data) and to workspace storage (the two workspace storage buckets and GCE persistent disks), the storage key to classic workspaces only.
claims.context: Customer-managed keys on Google Cloud; tier and region requirements must be verified.

claims.description: A VPC Service Controls service perimeter describes a set of Google Cloud resources that exchange data freely among themselves; a request whose source is inside the perimeter and whose target is outside is blocked; the Databricks SDK's endpoint rule model includes an option covering all Google APIs that support VPC Service Controls.
claims.context: Perimeter behaviour from Google's API description; Databricks support is not stated in the read sources.

claims.description: Policy Troubleshooter lists the IAM policies evaluated to check a principal's permission, including policies inherited from the organization, folder and project; Cloud Storage's testIamPermissions reports which permissions the caller itself holds on a bucket.

Databricks' Unity Catalog guide for Google Cloud grants, for file events, a custom role with Pub/Sub topic and subscription permissions and storage.buckets.update to the storage credential's service account at project level, and roles/pubsub.publisher to the project's Cloud Storage service account.
claims.context: Unity Catalog file events on Google Cloud; the permission set must be read from the current guide.

concepts.definition: Google Cloud's nesting of an organization root node, folders that organize its resources, and projects that contain resources, along which policies are inherited.
concepts.example: Bucket gs://cl-quality-raw sits in project cl-data-lake, in folder manufacturing, in Cinderline's organization.

concepts.definition: A policy that sets a constraint on how Google Cloud resources may be configured, inherited down the hierarchy and overridable where the constraint allows.
concepts.example: A folder policy allowing only EU locations refuses resources in us-east4 even for the project owner.

concepts.definition: The Google Cloud project a classic workspace names, which Databricks uses to create the workspace's cloud resources.
concepts.example: cinderline-gcp-prod names project cl-dbx-prod, where its VMs and workspace buckets are created.

concepts.definition: Where Databricks compute runs: Compute Engine VMs in the customer's project for classic, Databricks-managed compute for serverless.
concepts.example: The nightly job runs on VMs in cl-dbx-prod, or on serverless compute that uses none of Cinderline's projects.

concepts.definition: A workspace created with compute mode SERVERLESS and a region, naming no customer project, network configuration or workspace buckets.
concepts.example: cinderline-gcp-sls in us-east4 names no Cinderline project at all.

concepts.definition: A Google Cloud identity for an application or VM rather than a person, owned by one project whose ID appears in its email.
concepts.example: dbx-provisioner@cl-admin-tools.iam.gserviceaccount.com is owned by project cl-admin-tools.

concepts.definition: The service account Databricks creates for a Google Cloud workspace, of the form db-<workspace-id>@prod-gcp-<region>.iam.gserviceaccount.com.
concepts.example: db-8811223344556677@prod-gcp-us-east4.iam.gserviceaccount.com for a workspace with synthetic ID 8811223344556677.

concepts.definition: A Unity Catalog object that, on Google Cloud, makes Databricks create a managed service account whose email is granted roles on buckets.
concepts.example: cred_quality returns an email that the bucket owner binds to roles on gs://cl-quality-raw.

concepts.definition: An IAM policy entry on a Cloud Storage bucket that grants a role to members such as a service account email.
concepts.example: serviceAccount:uc-cred-quality@example-dbx-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com bound to roles/storage.legacyBucketReader on gs://cl-quality-raw.

concepts.definition: A VPC the customer provides at workspace creation, registered with its project, VPC and one regional subnet for classic compute nodes.
concepts.example: cl-vpc-dbx in cl-net-host with subnet dbx-nodes-use4 (10.20.0.0/22) in us-east4.

concepts.definition: A subnet setting that lets VMs without external IP addresses reach Google APIs and services.
concepts.example: dbx-nodes-use4 has it on, so nodes read gs:// buckets without Cloud NAT.

concepts.definition: A NAT service configured on a Cloud Router that lets VMs in chosen subnets reach the internet without external IP addresses.
concepts.example: cl-nat-use4 on cl-router-use4 translates every range of the node subnet.

concepts.definition: A network-level rule that allows or denies ingress or egress for matching instances, settled by the lowest priority number.
concepts.example: deny-all-egress at 65000 and allow-psc-endpoints at 1000 in cl-vpc-dbx.

concepts.definition: The control-plane endpoint that classic cluster nodes connect out to, named tunnel.<region>.gcp.databricks.com in Databricks' PSC template.
concepts.example: Nodes in dbx-nodes-use4 open their tunnel to tunnel.us-east4.gcp.databricks.com.

concepts.term: Private Service Connect (Databricks on Google Cloud)
concepts.definition: Private connectivity in which a forwarding rule in the customer's VPC targets a Databricks service attachment and is registered in the Databricks account.
concepts.example: relay-pe at 10.20.8.5 forwards to the relay service attachment and is registered as the dataplane_relay endpoint.

concepts.definition: An account object attached to a workspace that sets whether public access is enabled and which registered endpoints may reach its UI and API.
concepts.example: cl-pas-use4 at ENDPOINT level admits only the transit VPC's front-end endpoint.

concepts.definition: A Cloud DNS zone visible only to listed VPC networks, used to answer Databricks hostnames with PSC endpoint addresses.
concepts.example: dbx-psc-zone answers tunnel.us-east4.gcp.databricks.com with 10.20.8.5 inside cl-vpc-dbx.

concepts.definition: A Databricks account object that governs connections from serverless compute to customer resources through default and target rules.
concepts.example: An NCC with a private endpoint rule is how serverless reaches private resources on AWS and Azure; on Google Cloud it is unknown until verified.

concepts.definition: A design status for a capability that no read source settles for the account, region and release, kept until a named source or test does.
concepts.example: Serverless private access to Cloud SQL stays unknown until the account team confirms it in writing.

concepts.definition: A table that asks each cloud the same deployment questions, with every answer sourced separately and never copied across columns.
concepts.example: The question 'what does the workspace name?' answered as a project, a credential role or an Azure resource.

concepts.definition: A fixed sequence of checks chosen by failure shape: follow the layer a refusal names, or walk the path outward for a timeout.
concepts.example: STORAGE_DENIED leads to the bucket's IAM policy; BOOTSTRAP_TIMEOUT leads to name resolution.

concepts.definition: A Cloud KMS key the customer supplies for Databricks managed services or workspace storage, used through a Databricks control-plane service account.
concepts.example: A key in Cinderline's key ring encrypting the two workspace buckets and node persistent disks.

concepts.definition: A boundary around Google Cloud projects inside which resources exchange data freely and across which outbound requests are blocked.
concepts.example: A perimeter around cl-data-lake refuses a copy to a bucket in a project outside it.

concepts.definition: A Google Cloud service that explains whether a principal holds a permission on a resource and which policies decided it.
concepts.example: Checking storage.objects.get for the credential's email on gs://cl-quality-raw.

concepts.definition: Bucket change notifications Unity Catalog can consume through Pub/Sub, which need extra project-level grants.
concepts.example: The credential's service account holds a custom Pub/Sub role in cl-data-lake.

visuals.alt: Egress rules for cl-vpc-dbx before and after a broad deny is added at priority 900, then the decision rule as an equation.

questions.prompt: Creating Cinderline's workspace in us-east4 fails with CONSTRAINT_VIOLATED (fictional text): folder manufacturing allows EU locations only. The platform lead holds the owner role on cl-dbx-prod. What is the accurate next step?

options.text: Read the effective organization policy on the folder and agree an exception or another region with its owner; an IAM role cannot override the constraint.
options.rationale: Correct: organization policies restrict configuration separately from IAM and are inherited down the hierarchy, so the fix sits with whoever owns the folder's policy.

options.text: Retry as project owner, because the owner role includes every permission in the project.
options.rationale: The owner already failed: IAM grants permissions, while the constraint restricts which configurations are allowed at all.

options.text: Ask a Databricks account admin to allow us-east4 in the account console.
options.rationale: The Databricks account sits outside Google's hierarchy and cannot change a Google Cloud organization policy.

options.text: Grant the workspace service account a broader role on the organization.
options.rationale: More IAM does not lift a configuration constraint, and a broad organization grant widens every project below it.

questions.prompt: Cinderline adds serverless workspace cinderline-gcp-sls in us-east4. Which of these must already exist in one of Cinderline's Google Cloud projects before it can be created?

options.text: Nothing: a serverless workspace needs no prerequisite resources and names no project or network configuration.
options.rationale: Correct: the provider documents compute_mode SERVERLESS with only a name and location, and Databricks' template skips the project container and network for it.

options.text: A customer-managed VPC with one subnet in us-east4.
options.rationale: That is a classic workspace's network hand-over; serverless workspaces carry no network configuration.

options.text: Two workspace storage buckets in a Cinderline project.
options.rationale: Workspace buckets belong to classic workspaces; a serverless workspace uses default storage managed by Databricks.

options.text: A Cloud NAT gateway so serverless compute can reach the control plane.
options.rationale: Cloud NAT is an outbound path for classic nodes in Cinderline's subnet; serverless compute uses no Cinderline subnet.

questions.prompt: Which of these service accounts is created in, and owned by, one of Cinderline's projects?

options.text: The provisioning account Cinderline created and added to the Databricks account console as an account admin.
options.rationale: Correct: Cinderline creates it in its own project (cl-admin-tools in the example), grants it the Workspace Creator role and lets named people impersonate it.

options.text: The workspace service account db-<workspace-id>@prod-gcp-<region>.iam.gserviceaccount.com.

beats.title: Policies set above your project still reach the workspace
beats.outcome: Place a workspace's project in Google Cloud's organization, folder and project hierarchy and name which inherited policy can refuse a request.
beats.explanation: Google Cloud nests resources: an [[dbxfe-gcp-hierarchy-concept|organization]] at the root, folders beneath it, projects inside those and resources inside projects. A classic Databricks workspace names one project, and the IAM policies evaluated there can include policies inherited from its folder and organization. [[dbxfe-gcp-orgpolicy-concept|Organization policies]] are a separate layer: constraints on configuration, also inherited downward. Notice in the second state that the project owner holds every IAM permission, yet the folder's location constraint still refuses the us-east4 resources the workspace needs.

samajh.text: Socho ek housing society hai: society (organization) ke andar wings (folders) aur har wing mein flats (projects). Flat ka owner apne ghar mein bahut kuch kar sakta hai, par society ka rule, jaise 'terrace par koi construction nahi', har flat par lagta hai, chahe owner ke paas har kamre ki chaabi ho. Databricks workspace ko jo flat diya gaya, wahi uska project hai, aur society ke rules uspar bhi lagte hain.
samajh.mapping: The society is the organization, the wings are folders, the flats are projects; society rules are organization policies that apply even when the flat owner's IAM role would allow the change.
samajh.boundary: IAM grants are also inherited downward, unlike household keys, and a lower level can override a policy where the constraint allows it; the exact evaluation rules are Google's, not the society's.

beats.hint: Ask which layer the refusal names: a missing permission, or a constraint.

handbook.markdown:
**What sits where.** Google's Resource Manager API describes the organization as the root node for a company's resources, folders as containers that organize them, and a project as the container for APIs, VMs and other resources; a project's parent is an organization or a folder. A classic workspace records exactly one project as its cloud resource container (`cloud_resource_container.gcp.project_id`), the project Databricks uses to create the workspace's cloud resources. Its network configuration records the VPC's own project separately (`network_project_id`), so the VPC can sit elsewhere in the tree. The Databricks account, reached at `accounts.gcp.databricks.com`, is not a node in Google's hierarchy at all.

**Two inherited layers.** IAM answers *who may do what*: Policy Troubleshooter's description says the policies evaluated for a permission include the resource's own policy and policies inherited from its project, folder and organization. Organization policies answer *which configurations are allowed*: constraints set on an organization, folder or project are inherited downward and can be overridden where the constraint permits. A project owner therefore cannot grant their way past a constraint.

**Worked example (synthetic).** Folder `manufacturing` allows EU locations; `cl-dbx-prod` sits in it; the workspace is planned in `us-east4`. The refusal names a constraint, not a missing permission, so the next move is the folder's effective policy and a conversation with its owner, not another role.

**What to inspect, read-only.**
```bash
gcloud projects get-ancestors cl-dbx-prod
gcloud org-policies list --project=cl-dbx-prod
```
The first lists the folder and organization chain; the second lists policies set on the project. Constraint names differ between organizations: read them from the error and the policy, never from this example. Command syntax is illustrative; check the current gcloud reference.

beats.recap: A project owner's IAM role cannot lift a constraint inherited from the folder or organization above.

beats.title: A classic workspace borrows your project; a serverless one needs none
beats.outcome: Assign each resource of a classic and a serverless workspace on Google Cloud to the party that operates it.
beats.explanation: A classic workspace names your project, and by default Databricks creates a VPC there. Its compute runs as Compute Engine VMs taking addresses from a subnet in that network, and its two workspace storage buckets sit in your project too. A [[dbxfe-gcp-serverless-workspace-concept|serverless workspace]] is created with a name, a region and compute mode SERVERLESS: no project container and no network configuration. Notice in the second table that serverless removes your VPC, NAT, firewall and workspace-bucket rows, but not the catalog grants and bucket roles for data you own.
beats.hint: List what the serverless workspace resource takes as arguments; everything else is not Cinderline's.

handbook.markdown:
**Classic.** The account API creates a classic workspace with a `location` (the region) and a `cloud_resource_container` naming the project Databricks uses to instantiate the workspace's cloud resources. Clusters are Compute Engine VMs whose addresses come from the network configuration's subnet (the provider calls them GCE cluster nodes). Databricks' reference architecture lists "the two workspace storage buckets and the GCE Persistent Disk volumes of compute resources" as workspace storage that a customer-managed key can protect, which places them with the classic workspace's project. By default Databricks creates a VPC in that project for each workspace; a customer-managed VPC must be chosen at creation, because an existing workspace cannot be migrated to one. A classic workspace reports the effective compute mode `HYBRID`: it can also use serverless compute where that is available.

**Serverless.** The same resource takes only a name, a location and `compute_mode = "SERVERLESS"`:
```hcl
resource "databricks_mws_workspaces" "sls" {
  account_id     = var.databricks_account_id
  workspace_name = "cinderline-gcp-sls"
  location       = "us-east4"
  compute_mode   = "SERVERLESS"
}
```
This is the documented shape, shown for reading; nothing is applied. Databricks' template gives such a workspace no project container and no network configuration, and the account API's storage modes include `DEFAULT_STORAGE`. The architecture overview places serverless compute in a Databricks-managed plane; that page could not be read in this build, so treat the placement as documented but re-verify it for Cinderline's region.

**What stays yours.** Unity Catalog grants, storage credentials and the IAM roles on Cinderline's own buckets serve both planes, because the catalog, not the compute, holds the credential. What changes is who operates the network and whether serverless can reach Cinderline's private sources at all: on Google Cloud that cell is unknown until verified (see the serverless beat).

beats.recap: Classic puts VMs, workspace buckets and the network in your project; serverless names no project, but your catalog grants and bucket roles still apply.

beats.title: One query crosses four paths, each with a named identity
beats.outcome: Trace the author, control, execution and storage paths of one query on Google Cloud and name the identity and owner at each hop.
beats.explanation: Follow the nightly quality query. Ana signs in to the workspace URL: the author path. The control plane schedules the job, which runs as service principal sp-quality-nightly, and Unity Catalog checks that principal's grants: the control path. A Compute Engine VM in cl-dbx-prod, or serverless compute, executes it. The read of gs://cl-quality-raw uses the storage credential's Databricks-managed [[dbxfe-gcp-sa-concept|service account]], which Cloud Storage authorizes by its bucket roles. Notice that no hop after sign-in uses Ana's identity, and serverless changes only the execution node.
beats.hint: After sign-in, whose identity does the catalog check, and whose does Cloud Storage check?

handbook.markdown:
**Author path.** Ana reaches the workspace URL over the public internet or, if Cinderline builds it, through a front-end Private Service Connect endpoint. Her identity authenticates her session; it does not travel with the job.

**Control path.** The job's run-as principal, `sp-quality-nightly`, is what Unity Catalog checks: `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA` and `SELECT` on the table, and `READ FILES` on the external location for file reads. A refusal here names that principal and a privilege.

**Execution path.** On classic compute, a Compute Engine VM in `cl-dbx-prod` takes an address from the registered subnet and opens an outbound tunnel to the secure cluster connectivity relay, through Cloud NAT or a back-end PSC endpoint. On serverless compute the VM, subnet and tunnel are not Cinderline's.

**Storage path.** The external location pairs `gs://cl-quality-raw/inspections/` with credential `cred_quality`, whose Databricks-managed service account reads the objects; Cloud Storage checks that account's roles on the bucket. Unity Catalog's temporary-credential API, which returns a short-lived Google OAuth token for a path, shows the pattern: the catalog holds the service account, and callers never see a key.

**Evidence to collect, read-only.**
```sql
SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE quality.raw.inspections;
DESCRIBE EXTERNAL LOCATION loc_quality_raw;
DESCRIBE STORAGE CREDENTIAL cred_quality;
```
Record the run-as principal from the job settings, the credential's service account email, and the bucket's IAM policy for that email. What this beat does not settle: which service account Databricks attaches to classic VMs by default and what it may read. That row stays unknown until verified, and it matters, because code on a VM can request tokens for the VM's own service account through the metadata server.

beats.recap: Author, control, execution and storage paths each carry their own identity; only execution changes between classic and serverless.

beats.title: A service account's email names the project that owns it
beats.outcome: Identify the owning project and purpose of each service account in a Databricks on Google Cloud deployment.
beats.explanation: Google builds a [[dbxfe-gcp-sa-concept|service account]]'s email from the project that owns it and a name, so read the table's second column that way. The provisioning account lives in Cinderline's cl-admin-tools. The [[dbxfe-gcp-workspace-sa-concept|workspace service account]], db-<workspace-id>@prod-gcp-<region>.iam.gserviceaccount.com, lives in a Databricks project. The storage credential's account is Databricks-managed, and the account used with a customer-managed key exists in the Databricks control-plane project. Notice the unknown row: which account Databricks attaches to classic VMs by default is not settled by the sources read here.

samajh.text: Office mein har visitor ke gate pass par us company ka naam chhapa hota hai jisne pass banwaya. Pass dekh ke pata chal jaata hai ki banda kis company ka hai, chahe woh kisi bhi floor par ghoom raha ho. Service account ki email bhi aisi hi hai: @ ke baad wala hissa batata hai ki kis project ne use banaya. db-...@prod-gcp-us-east4 Databricks ka pass hai, Cinderline ka nahi; par Cinderline ke floor par entry dena Cinderline ke haath mein hai.
samajh.mapping: The gate pass is the service account email, the company printed on it is the owning project in the email domain, and the floors it may enter are the roles granted on each Cinderline resource.
samajh.boundary: A pass shows who issued it, not what it may open; permissions come only from IAM bindings on each resource, and Google-managed service agents use other email formats.

beats.hint: Look at the part of each email after the @ sign.

handbook.markdown:
**Reading an email.** Google's IAM API says the creator of a service account names the owning project and an account name, and IAM builds the email from them; the account's `projectId` is the owner. `dbx-provisioner@cl-admin-tools.iam.gserviceaccount.com` is therefore Cinderline's, and `db-8811223344556677@prod-gcp-us-east4.iam.gserviceaccount.com` (synthetic workspace ID, documented format) is owned by `prod-gcp-us-east4`, a Databricks project.

**Provisioner.** Databricks' Google Cloud guide creates this account in the customer's project, adds it to the account console as an account admin and lets listed people impersonate it through `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator`. Account APIs accept only Google-issued OIDC tokens. Its custom Workspace Creator role is evidence of what creation touches: creating IAM roles and service accounts, reading and setting the project's IAM policy, enabling services, reading networks, setting subnetwork IAM, creating firewall rules, and reading forwarding rules for PSC.

**Workspace account.** Databricks creates it per workspace. Given the creator's permission to set the project's IAM policy, expect it to hold roles in Cinderline's project after creation; which roles is unknown until verified, so capture the project IAM policy before and after creation.

**Storage credential account.** The SDK calls it a Databricks-created Google Cloud Storage service account with a credential ID and an email; Cinderline binds that email on buckets.

**Key account.** For a customer-managed key, the API says the service account with access to the key exists within the Databricks control-plane project; with `manual` set, Databricks will not use OAuth to grant itself access, and Cinderline grants it.

**Cluster account.** A classic cluster's `gcp_attributes.google_service_account` authenticates the cluster to Cloud Storage and BigQuery. Compute Engine attaches at most one service account per VM, and code on the VM reads its tokens through the metadata server, so every workload on that cluster acts as that account.

beats.recap: Read a service account's owner off its email domain, then find the grant it needs on something Cinderline owns.

beats.title: A Unity Catalog credential is a service account waiting for bucket roles
beats.outcome: Set up, in order, the Unity Catalog and Cloud Storage objects that let a Google Cloud bucket be read through an external location.
beats.explanation: On Google Cloud, creating a [[dbxfe-gcp-credential-concept|storage credential]] makes Databricks create a Databricks-managed service account and return its email. Nothing can be read yet: someone who administers the Cloud Storage (GCS) bucket must [[dbxfe-gcp-bucket-iam-concept|bind that email]] to roles on it, and Databricks' Unity Catalog guide binds Storage Object Admin and Storage Legacy Bucket Reader. An external location then pairs a gs:// path with the credential, and catalog privileges decide which principals may use it. Notice in the second state that a cluster's own Google service account reaches the same bucket while skipping the catalog check.
beats.hint: Which system checks the bucket roles, and which one checks READ FILES?

handbook.markdown:
**Order of operations.**
1. Create the credential; Databricks creates the service account and returns its email (output only).
2. On the bucket, its administrator binds that email to roles. Databricks' guide uses these, shown in its Terraform shape:
```hcl
resource "databricks_storage_credential" "quality" {
  name = "cred_quality"
  databricks_gcp_service_account {}
}
resource "google_storage_bucket_iam_member" "reader" {
  bucket = "cl-quality-raw"
  role   = "roles/storage.legacyBucketReader"
  member = "serviceAccount:${databricks_storage_credential.quality.databricks_gcp_service_account[0].email}"
}
```
(the guide adds `roles/storage.objectAdmin` the same way). These roles also permit writes; if the use is read-only, compare the credential's `read_only` option and the current Databricks page's minimum roles before copying them. That minimum is unknown here.
3. Create the external location and grant its use:
```sql
CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION loc_quality_raw
  URL 'gs://cl-quality-raw/inspections/'
  WITH (STORAGE CREDENTIAL cred_quality);
GRANT READ FILES ON EXTERNAL LOCATION loc_quality_raw TO `quality-jobs`;
```

**Why the order matters.** Cloud Storage knows nothing about catalog grants, and the catalog cannot create Google bindings. With uniform bucket-level access, only bucket-level or higher IAM policies decide access, so the binding can also arrive from the project, folder or organization: check upward before adding another.

**Cross-project and cross-organization buckets.** The service account can be bound on any bucket its administrator controls. A supplier's bucket needs the supplier's administrator, under the supplier's organization policies; Cinderline cannot make that grant.

**The legacy pattern.** A classic cluster's `google_service_account` authenticates that cluster to Cloud Storage and BigQuery. Every workload on the cluster then reads with that account's roles, and the catalog's grants are not the gate. How current access modes treat such direct reads is on the access-mode pages; read them before relying on either behaviour.

**Troubleshooting.** A recreated credential should be expected to have a new service account email, so old bindings do not carry over: compare the email in `DESCRIBE STORAGE CREDENTIAL` with the bucket policy before anything else.

beats.recap: Create the credential, bind its email on the bucket, then create the external location and grant its use.

beats.title: Classic compute needs one regional subnet and a way out
beats.outcome: List what a customer-managed VPC must hand a classic workspace on Google Cloud and predict the failure when its outbound path is removed.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-gcp-vpc-concept|customer-managed VPC]] is registered as a network configuration naming the VPC's project, the VPC and one subnet in the workspace's region. Compute Engine nodes take their addresses from that subnet, whose netmask must fall between /29 and /9 and which no other workspace or resource may share. Nodes need outbound access through [[dbxfe-gcp-nat-concept|Cloud NAT]] or a similar appliance unless back-end PSC carries control-plane traffic. Notice in the second state that deleting the NAT stops cluster starts while the subnet, Private Google Access and firewall rules look unchanged.
beats.hint: Which direction does a classic node open its connection to the control plane?

handbook.markdown:
**What the network configuration pins.** The provider's `gcp_network_info` block names `network_project_id` (the project where the VPC and subnet reside), `vpc_id`, `subnet_id` and `subnet_region`. The documented requirements: the subnet is in the workspace's region and its range allocates the GCE cluster nodes; its netmask is between /29 and /9; it has outbound access to the public network through Cloud NAT or a similar customer-managed appliance. One VPC can host several workspaces, but a subnet cannot be reused by other workspaces or non-Databricks resources, and a network configuration cannot be reused across workspaces. The secondary pod and service ranges of the older GKE-based design are deprecated and no longer supported.

**Documented shape, for reading (nothing is applied):**
```hcl
resource "google_compute_subnetwork" "nodes" {
  name                     = "dbx-nodes-use4"
  ip_cidr_range            = "10.20.0.0/22"
  region                   = "us-east4"
  network                  = google_compute_network.dbx.id
  private_ip_google_access = true
}
resource "databricks_mws_networks" "this" {
  account_id   = var.databricks_account_id
  network_name = "cl-net-use4"
  gcp_network_info {
    network_project_id = "cl-net-host"
    vpc_id             = "cl-vpc-dbx"
    subnet_id          = "dbx-nodes-use4"
    subnet_region      = "us-east4"
  }
}
```
Databricks' guide creates the Cloud Router and NAT before the workspace, commenting that this makes sure the NAT exists for outbound traffic.

**Failure shape.** Nodes dial out to the relay, so a missing outbound path appears as a start that never completes: no principal, no permission, no refusal. Work outward: NAT coverage of the subnet, the relay name's answer from the subnet, egress firewall rules by priority.

**Evidence, read-only.**
```bash
gcloud compute networks subnets describe dbx-nodes-use4 --region=us-east4 --project=cl-net-host
gcloud compute routers nats list --router=cl-router-use4 --region=us-east4 --project=cl-net-host
```
**Not settled here:** whether Private Google Access is required rather than merely set in Databricks' examples, subnet sizing per node, and shared-network (host project) requirements. Each is unknown until verified on the customer-managed VPC page.

beats.recap: One regional subnet (/29 to /9) that nothing else shares, plus an outbound path; removing the NAT stalls starts without any refusal.

beats.title: Private Google Access, Cloud NAT and PSC carry different destinations
beats.outcome: Predict which outbound destinations a classic node can reach with and without Cloud NAT when back-end PSC is used.
beats.explanation: Three mechanisms answer three kinds of destination. [[dbxfe-gcp-pga-concept|Private Google Access]] lets nodes without external addresses reach Google APIs such as Cloud Storage. Cloud NAT carries traffic to the public internet. Back-end PSC endpoints carry control-plane traffic on private addresses. Databricks' reference template creates no Cloud NAT when back-end PSC is enabled, and the second table shows the consequence: the relay, the REST API and gs:// reads still work, but a public package index is unreachable until someone designs a mirror or an explicit egress path.
beats.hint: Sort the destinations into Google APIs, the Databricks control plane and everything else.

handbook.markdown:
**Three definitions, from Google's Compute Engine API.** A subnet's `privateIpGoogleAccess` says whether VMs in it can access Google services without assigned external IP addresses. A Cloud Router NAT enables VMs in the chosen subnetworks to access the internet without external IP addresses. An instance with no access configuration has no external internet access. Classic nodes need those mechanisms because they are reached through the paths their subnet provides.

**Without PSC.** Databricks requires outbound access to the public network through Cloud NAT or a similar appliance, and its guide builds the NAT before the workspace. Control-plane and relay traffic leave through the NAT to public addresses; so does any library download or external API call.

**With back-end PSC.** Databricks' reference template skips the Cloud Router and NAT when PSC is enabled, keeps Private Google Access on its subnets, and resolves the workspace and relay names to private endpoint addresses. Its README's stated aim is that classic compute to control plane traffic does not travel over the public internet. The side effect is a design decision you must make on purpose: public package indexes, internet data sources and external APIs have no path. Options include a private package mirror, a proxy with an allowlist, or a NAT kept deliberately with egress firewall rules that name what may leave.

**Evidence, read-only.** The subnet's Private Google Access flag; the list of routers and NATs in the region (an empty list is evidence too); a timed test from a notebook, for example:
```bash
curl -sS -m 10 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://pypi.org/simple/
```
A timeout with no HTTP status is a missing path; an HTTP error is a reply from something that received the request.

**Not settled here:** which Google APIs besides Cloud Storage classic nodes need, and whether restricted Google API endpoints or VPC Service Controls change these paths for Databricks. Both are unknown until verified.

beats.recap: Private Google Access reaches Google APIs, Cloud NAT reaches the internet, PSC reaches the control plane; drop the NAT and only the internet path disappears.

beats.title: The lowest priority number wins across the whole network
beats.outcome: Predict which Google Cloud firewall rule decides a connection and explain why priority, not address specificity, settles it.
beats.explanation: A Google Cloud [[dbxfe-gcp-firewall-concept|firewall rule]] belongs to a VPC network, not to one instance: it applies to every VM in the network unless target tags or target service accounts narrow it. When several rules match a connection, the rule with the lowest priority number decides, and at equal priority a deny beats an allow; implied rules sit at 65535. Notice in the second table that a broad deny at priority 900 overrides the narrower allow at 1000, cutting nodes off from the PSC endpoints even though the allow names their exact range.
beats.hint: Sort the matching rules by priority number, not by how narrow their ranges are.

handbook.markdown:
**The mechanism, from Google's Compute Engine API.** A firewall rule allows or denies ingress or egress traffic for instances in one VPC network. Direction defaults to `INGRESS`. Priority runs from 0 to 65535 with 1000 as the default; lower values take precedence, and at equal priority `DENY` beats `ALLOW`. The network has implied rules at priority 65535, so explicit rules should use lower numbers. `targetTags` or `targetServiceAccounts` restrict which instances a rule applies to; with neither, it applies to every instance in the network. Rules can log matches to Cloud Logging.

**Worked example (synthetic).** A hardened design keeps `deny-all-egress` at 65000 and opens what nodes need at 1000. A colleague later adds `block-internet` at 900 to stop internet traffic. Because it matches every destination and has the lowest number, it decides every egress connection, and the relay tunnel fails exactly as a missing NAT would. The fix is ordering: the allows need lower numbers than any broad deny, or the deny needs narrower ranges.

**What Databricks' sources show.** The Workspace Creator role includes permission to read and create firewall rules, so expect workspace creation to create rules in the VPC's project. Databricks' reference template creates an ingress rule for the Databricks subnet before creating the workspace and, when network hardening is on without PSC, an egress rule to the region's control-plane IP addresses, published per region. The exact rules Databricks requires, their ports and the address lists are on the customer-managed VPC page and remain unknown until verified.

**Evidence, read-only.**
```bash
gcloud compute firewall-rules list --project=cl-net-host --filter="network~cl-vpc-dbx" --sort-by=priority
```
Also list any organization or network firewall policies attached above the VPC: Compute Engine models them as separate resources, and a rule there can decide a connection before you look at the VPC's own list.

beats.recap: Among matching rules the lowest priority number decides, a deny wins a tie, and rules without targets cover every VM in the network.

beats.title: Back-end PSC is two registered endpoints and private DNS names
beats.outcome: Assemble the objects back-end Private Service Connect needs on both sides and name the DNS records that make them usable.
beats.explanation: Back-end [[dbxfe-gcp-psc-concept|Private Service Connect]] gives classic nodes two private addresses in your VPC: one for the [[dbxfe-gcp-scc-concept|secure cluster connectivity relay]] and one for the REST API. Each is a forwarding rule targeting a Databricks service attachment, registered in the Databricks account by project, endpoint name and region, and listed in the network configuration as dataplane_relay or rest_api. Nodes only use them if names resolve privately: Databricks' reference template adds a [[dbxfe-gcp-dns-concept|private zone]] for gcp.databricks.com. Notice the second state: without the tunnel record, bootstrap stalls.

samajh.text: Maano Cinderline ki factory ke andar ek supplier ne apni khidki khol di hai: andar se hi baat ho jaati hai, bahar sadak par jaane ki zaroorat nahi. Par factory ki directory mein us khidki ka number likha hona chahiye. Agar directory abhi bhi supplier ka purana sadak wala pata batati hai, toh worker bahar jaane ki koshish karega, gate band milega, aur khidki khuli hone ke bawajood kaam atka rahega.
samajh.mapping: The inside window is a PSC endpoint address in Cinderline's VPC, the supplier behind it is the Databricks service attachment, and the factory directory is the private DNS zone that must list the window.
samajh.boundary: A PSC endpoint forwards packets to a producer's load balancer and has no staff or queue; whether a connection is accepted is governed by the producer's accept list and registration, not by anyone at a window.

beats.hint: Count the endpoints, then count the hostnames that must point at them.

handbook.markdown:
**Google Cloud side.** A PSC endpoint is a forwarding rule whose target is a producer's service attachment; Google's API says a PSC forwarding rule to a managed service must target a service attachment, and reports a `pscConnectionStatus` of `ACCEPTED`, `PENDING`, `REJECTED`, `CLOSED` or `NEEDS_ATTENTION`. Databricks' reference template reserves two internal addresses in a small endpoint subnet (with Private Google Access on), creates `relay-pe` and `workspace-pe` targeting the region's relay and workspace service attachments, and adds a private Cloud DNS zone for `gcp.databricks.com`, visible to the workspace VPC, with A records for the workspace URL (`<workspace-id>.<last digit>.gcp.databricks.com`), its `dp-` variant and `tunnel.<region>.gcp.databricks.com`, the name cluster VMs use to open the secure tunnel. Its README calls these zones required for back-end PSC.

**Databricks side.** Each endpoint is registered as a VPC endpoint object, then referenced by the network configuration (documented shape, for reading):
```hcl
resource "databricks_mws_vpc_endpoint" "relay" {
  account_id        = var.databricks_account_id
  vpc_endpoint_name = "cl-relay-use4"
  gcp_vpc_endpoint_info {
    project_id        = "cl-net-host"
    psc_endpoint_name = "relay-pe"
    endpoint_region   = "us-east4"
  }
}
# network configuration: vpc_endpoints { dataplane_relay = [relay id], rest_api = [workspace-pe id] }
```
Registration exports `psc_connection_id` and `service_attachment_id`. The workspace must be created with a private access settings object to support any PSC scenario, a customer-managed VPC is required, and the provisioning account needs `compute.forwardingRules.get` and `list`.

**Evidence, read-only.**
```bash
gcloud compute forwarding-rules describe relay-pe --region=us-east4 --project=cl-net-host --format="value(pscConnectionStatus)"
gcloud dns record-sets list --zone=dbx-psc-zone --project=cl-net-host
```
**Not settled here:** the service attachment URIs per region, whether Cinderline's account or project must be enabled before connections are accepted, and tier requirements. They are on the PSC page, unknown until verified.

beats.recap: Two forwarding rules to Databricks' service attachments, registered and listed in the network configuration, and a private zone that answers their names.

beats.title: Private access settings decide which endpoints reach the workspace
beats.outcome: Predict whether a user request reaches the workspace from the access level, the endpoint used and whether public access is enabled.
beats.explanation: Front-end PSC puts an endpoint in a transit VPC so users reach the web application, REST API and Databricks Connect privately. What may connect is decided by the workspace's [[dbxfe-gcp-pas-concept|private access settings]]. ACCOUNT level admits any VPC endpoint registered in the Databricks account; ENDPOINT level admits only the listed endpoint IDs. Public access defaults to enabled on Google Cloud, unlike AWS, and while it is enabled an IP access list is the control for public sources. Notice how the contractor's registered endpoint gets in under ACCOUNT and is refused under ENDPOINT.
beats.hint: Ask which list, if any, the access level consults.

handbook.markdown:
**The object.** Private access settings are an account object attached to a workspace, and a workspace must be created with one to support any PSC scenario. Documented fields: `public_access_enabled` (default `true` on Google Cloud, `false` on AWS); `private_access_level`, `ACCOUNT` by default, admitting only VPC endpoints registered in the Databricks account, or `ENDPOINT`, admitting only `allowed_vpc_endpoint_ids`; and the region. With public access enabled, IP access lists restrict public sources. The API description, worded for AWS, allows disabling public access only when both front-end and back-end private connections exist; verify that condition for Google Cloud before promising a fully private workspace.

**Documented shape, for reading (nothing is applied):**
```hcl
resource "databricks_mws_private_access_settings" "pas" {
  account_id                   = var.databricks_account_id
  private_access_settings_name = "cl-pas-use4"
  region                       = "us-east4"
  public_access_enabled        = false
  private_access_level         = "ENDPOINT"
  allowed_vpc_endpoint_ids     = [databricks_mws_vpc_endpoint.frontend.vpc_endpoint_id]
}
```

**The user path.** Databricks' PSC guide places the front-end endpoint in a transit (bastion) VPC that users reach, for example over VPN, and uses it for the web application, REST API and Databricks Connect API. Users' resolvers must answer the workspace URL with that endpoint's internal address inside the transit network; the exact records are on the PSC page and are unknown here until verified.

**Why ACCOUNT can surprise.** Every endpoint registered anywhere in the Databricks account passes ACCOUNT level, including one registered for another team's workspace. ENDPOINT level turns the settings into an explicit allow list.

**Evidence.** The workspace's private access settings ID, the object's level, public-access flag and allow list from the account API, the IP access list configuration, and the registered endpoints with their projects. Whether a running workspace's settings can be changed on Google Cloud is not settled in the sources read here (the provider lists updatable fields generally and a separate list for AWS); treat it as unknown.

beats.recap: ACCOUNT admits every endpoint registered in the account, ENDPOINT only the listed ones, and public access stays on by default on Google Cloud.

beats.title: Serverless private connectivity on Google Cloud stays unknown until verified
beats.outcome: Separate what the read sources show about serverless connectivity on Google Cloud from what must be verified, and write the unknown cells honestly.
beats.explanation: On AWS and Azure, serverless compute reaches private resources through [[dbxfe-gcp-ncc-concept|network connectivity configurations]]. For Google Cloud the evidence read in this build conflicts: the Terraform provider's documentation says NCC binding is available for AWS and Azure only, while the Python SDK's API model already carries a gcp_endpoint on private endpoint rules, and network policies list Google Cloud Storage destinations. A field in a schema is not availability in your account and region. Notice that the second table keeps every such cell [[dbxfe-gcp-unknown-concept|unknown until verified]] and plans a fallback.
beats.hint: Which of the read sources is the product page for Google Cloud?

handbook.markdown:
**What the sources say.** The provider documentation at v1.133.0 says the NCC binding "is available for AWS & Azure only, and is in Public Preview in AWS", and that NCC private endpoint rules are available on Azure and in Public Preview on AWS. Its NCC resource documents default rules for AWS (stable IP ranges) and Azure (service endpoints) and target rules for Azure and AWS private endpoints, with no Google Cloud variant. The Python SDK at v0.141.0, published the same week, models a `gcp_endpoint` on private endpoint rules: a target service attachment such as `projects/<project>/regions/us-east4/serviceAttachments/<name>`, selected Google API hostnames such as `storage.googleapis.com`, an option covering all Google APIs that support VPC Service Controls, and an output PSC endpoint URI. The network policy API lists `GOOGLE_CLOUD_STORAGE` among storage destination types.

**How to read the conflict.** Generated SDKs follow the API definition, and API fields can exist ahead of, behind or apart from what an account can use. Provider documentation can lag the product. Neither is the product page for Google Cloud, which this build could not read. So the honest reading is not "supported" and not "impossible": it is unknown until verified, with the evidence recorded.

**What verification looks like, without provisioning.** Read the current Databricks serverless networking page for Google Cloud; ask the account team for written confirmation naming region, tier and release status; list the account's existing NCC and network policy objects through the account API (read-only calls). A dry run of a network policy, where documented, is a later step owned by an account admin.

**The fallback.** Keep sources that live on private addresses in Cinderline's VPC, such as a Cloud SQL lookup, on classic compute until the cell closes. Serverless jobs that read only Cinderline's buckets through Unity Catalog need no private network path of Cinderline's.

**What not to write.** Do not copy the AWS or Azure answer into the Google Cloud column, do not cite an SDK field as availability, and do not upgrade a cell without a dated source.

beats.recap: A provider note says AWS and Azure only while the SDK models GCP endpoint rules, so serverless private connectivity on Google Cloud stays unknown until verified.

beats.title: Same questions get different answers than on AWS and Azure
beats.outcome: List the deployment questions whose Google Cloud answers differ from AWS and Azure and cite where each answer comes from.
beats.explanation: Ask each cloud the same questions, a [[dbxfe-gcp-matrix-concept|common questions matrix]], and keep the answers separate. On Google Cloud a classic workspace names a project, takes one regional subnet and filters traffic with network-wide firewall rules; on AWS it takes a credential role, a storage configuration and two subnets in different availability zones behind security groups; on Azure the workspace is itself an Azure resource whose injected network uses two delegated subnets. Storage identity differs too. Notice in the second table that private-connectivity defaults differ and one Google Cloud cell is still unknown.
beats.hint: For each row, ask which object exists on Google Cloud, not what it would be called.

handbook.markdown:
**Why a separate matrix.** Relabelling one cloud's diagram produces confident wrong answers: "security group" has no Google Cloud object, "trust policy" has no Google Cloud storage-credential equivalent, and a PSC endpoint is registered differently from a PrivateLink endpoint. The same questions, answered per cloud from that cloud's sources, keep the difference visible.

**Where the answers come from.** Google Cloud: the provider's Google Cloud guides and resource pages (project container, one subnet in the workspace region with a /29 to /9 netmask, Cloud NAT, VPC endpoints registered by project, endpoint name and region, `public_access_enabled` defaulting to true), Google's Compute Engine API (network-wide firewall rules by priority) and Databricks' reference template (private `gcp.databricks.com` zone). AWS, for contrast only: the provider's network resource (at least two subnets in different availability zones, /17 to /25, security groups), its storage credential resource (an IAM role that requires a trust policy) and its private access settings (public access disabled by default). Azure, for contrast only: the provider's Private Link guide (an `azurerm_databricks_workspace` resource in a resource group, subnets delegated to `Microsoft.Databricks/workspaces` with network security groups, private endpoints for back-end, front-end and browser authentication, public access set on the workspace resource) and the storage credential resource (an access connector's managed identity).

**Serverless rows.** The provider documents NCC binding for AWS and Azure only (Public Preview on AWS) and default egress rules for AWS stable IP ranges and Azure service endpoints; no Google Cloud variant is documented. The Google Cloud cells therefore read "unknown until verified" and "none documented", not a borrowed answer.

**Using it.** The AWS and Azure modules keep their own sourced answers to the same questions, and the three-cloud diagnosis lab practises them side by side. A Google Cloud cell is filled only from a Google Cloud source; an empty or unknown cell is a verification item with an owner, never a copy from the next column.

beats.recap: Answer each cloud's questions from that cloud's sources: project and one subnet on Google Cloud, not AWS's two subnets or Azure's delegated pair.

beats.title: A refusal names its layer, so read it before changing a grant
beats.outcome: Run an ordered diagnosis for a denied request on Google Cloud, starting from the layer the error names.
beats.explanation: A denial helps a diagnosis: some layer received the request and said no, so read whom it names. A catalog refusal names the job's principal and a privilege, and storage was never consulted. A Cloud Storage refusal names the credential's service account and a Google permission such as storage.objects.get, which means the catalog already agreed. Notice the two [[dbxfe-gcp-diagnosis-concept|ordered diagnoses]] in the timeline: the first stops at step three with a catalog grant; the second skips past the catalog to the bucket's [[dbxfe-gcp-bucket-iam-concept|IAM policy]], where the binding sits on the wrong bucket.
beats.hint: Is the name in the error a Databricks principal or a Google service account?

handbook.markdown:
**The sequence and why it is ordered.** Each step either eliminates a layer or finds the refusing one, and none changes anything until step six.
1. Record the exact error text, time and run ID. Which layer is named: a catalog privilege, a Google permission, or a constraint?
2. Confirm the acting principal: the job's run-as principal, not the author. For storage errors, note which service account is named.
3. Catalog privileges, if the catalog refused: `SHOW GRANTS` on the catalog, schema, table and external location.
4. Credential and binding, if Cloud Storage refused: `DESCRIBE STORAGE CREDENTIAL cred_quality` for the email, then the bucket's policy:
```bash
gcloud storage buckets get-iam-policy gs://cl-quality-raw
```
5. Inherited and organization policies: Policy Troubleshooter evaluates one principal, permission and resource and lists the policies consulted, including those inherited from the project, folder and organization:
```bash
gcloud policy-troubleshoot iam //storage.googleapis.com/projects/_/buckets/cl-quality-raw \
  --principal-email=uc-cred-quality@example-dbx-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --permission=storage.objects.get
```
A constraint refusal names the constraint instead and belongs to the policy's owner.
6. Make the smallest grant at the layer that refused, then rerun as the same principal.
7. Write the evidence row: error, principal or account, resource, binding or grant, rerun result.

**Traps.** Cloud Storage's `testIamPermissions` reports the caller's own permissions, so it cannot speak for a Databricks-managed account; use Policy Troubleshooter for that. A recreated credential should be expected to carry a new service account email, which is why step four compares emails before looking at roles. Granting a project-wide storage admin role "to be safe" hides the fault, widens every bucket in the project and is itself a finding. Command syntax here is illustrative; check the current gcloud reference.

beats.recap: Start from the layer the refusal names: a catalog privilege, a Google permission on a named account, or a constraint.

beats.title: A timeout names no layer, so walk the path outward
beats.outcome: Run an ordered diagnosis for an unreachable request on Google Cloud, from name resolution to endpoint status to firewall priority.
beats.explanation: An unreachable request leaves no refusal to read: no principal, no permission, just a timeout. So walk the path in the order packets travel. From a VM in the node subnet, what does the relay name resolve to? Is that address a PSC endpoint the producer has accepted? Does any egress rule with a lower priority number deny it? Notice the two states: first the [[dbxfe-gcp-dns-concept|private zone]] is visible to the wrong network, so the name answers publicly; after that fix, a deny at priority 900 still decides before the allow at 1000.

samajh.text: Courier wala parcel lekar nikla, par pata galat likha tha. Woh ghoomta raha, kisi ne mana nahi kiya, bas parcel pahuncha hi nahi. 'Mana karna' ek jawab hota hai jo kisi ne diya; 'pahuncha hi nahi' mein koi jawab nahi hota. Isliye pehle pata sahi hai ya nahi (DNS), phir kya darwaza khula hai (endpoint), phir kisi ne raasta toh nahi roka (firewall).
samajh.mapping: A refusal is a reply from a layer that received the request; a timeout means none did, so the diagnosis walks the path: the address, then the endpoint, then the firewall.
samajh.boundary: Networks can also reject quickly, with a reset or a logged deny, so speed alone does not classify a failure; read the error text and the logs, not only the elapsed time.

beats.hint: What does the relay name resolve to from inside the node subnet?

handbook.markdown:
**The sequence.** Follow the packet; each hop is read-only and cheap.
1. Record the symptom: a timeout, the cluster and the time. No principal is named, which is itself evidence that no layer received the request.
2. Note what changed: PSC enabled, NAT removed, zones created, rules added. Changes point, they do not prove.
3. Resolve the relay and workspace names from the node subnet, for example from a notebook on a running cluster in that subnet or a test VM the network team places there:
```bash
getent hosts tunnel.us-east4.gcp.databricks.com
```
4. If the answer is public, check the zone's visibility (Cloud DNS private zones are visible only to the networks listed) and its records:
```bash
gcloud dns managed-zones describe dbx-psc-zone --project=cl-net-host --format="value(privateVisibilityConfig.networks)"
```
5. If the answer is the endpoint's address, read the endpoint's `pscConnectionStatus`. `ACCEPTED` is healthy; `PENDING` means pending acceptance by the producer, and why Databricks has not accepted it (registration, enablement) is a question for the PSC page and the account team, unknown until verified.
6. Egress rules by priority for the node network, plus any firewall policies attached above it.
7. Retest one start and write every fault found, not only the last.

**Why this order.** Each hop depends on the previous: a status check is meaningless while the name points elsewhere, and a rule check is premature while the endpoint is not accepted. The second state shows why the row lists both faults: fixing DNS exposed a deny that had been hidden behind it.

**What not to do.** Granting IAM roles, opening ingress rules and recreating the workspace all change things a timeout never implicated. Adding a NAT back may make starts succeed through the public path while the private design stays broken; note it as a workaround, not a fix.

beats.recap: With no refusal to read, resolve the name, check the endpoint's status, then the egress rules by priority, and record every fault found.

beats.title: An evidence matrix keeps its unknown cells visible
beats.outcome: Assemble a Google Cloud permissions and network evidence matrix in which every unverified capability stays marked unknown.
beats.explanation: A design note is only as good as its evidence. Each row of the matrix names a boundary, the artefact that proves it, where that artefact lives and its status. Most rows can be captured read-only from Google Cloud or the Databricks account: bucket IAM policies, subnet settings, NAT configuration, endpoint status, zone visibility and private access settings. Notice the rows that stay [[dbxfe-gcp-unknown-concept|unknown until verified]]: the default VM service account, the required firewall rules, serverless private connectivity and tier requirements. They stay unknown until a named source or test settles them.
beats.hint: For each row, ask what artefact would prove it and who can read that artefact today.

handbook.markdown:
**Status vocabulary.** Use four words and keep them distinct:
- **Captured:** the artefact is in the record, with date and source.
- **Capture:** a read-only artefact exists and has an owner, but is not yet collected.
- **Unknown until verified:** no read source settles the capability for this account, region and release; the row names the source or test that would.
- **Not applicable:** the row does not exist for this plane (a serverless workspace has no subnet row).

**Rules.** A row moves from Unknown only with a dated source (a documentation page read, an account-team answer in writing, a test result); a Terraform example, an SDK field or another cloud's answer never moves it. Each row proves one layer: a permission row says nothing about reachability, a network row nothing about permission. Every row has an owner.

**Where the captures come from, all read-only.** Job settings and audit logs for the acting principal; `SHOW GRANTS` and `DESCRIBE STORAGE CREDENTIAL` for the catalog rows; the bucket's IAM policy and Policy Troubleshooter for storage; the subnet description, router NAT list and firewall list for the classic network; forwarding rule status and managed zone visibility for PSC; the account API for private access settings, network configurations and registered endpoints.

**Unknown rows in this build.** The default classic VM service account and its roles; the workspace account's roles in Cinderline's project; the firewall rules and Private Google Access requirement for customer-managed VPCs; serverless private connectivity on Google Cloud; PSC service attachment URIs per region; tier and region requirements for PSC and customer-managed keys. Each is recorded, not guessed.

**How it is used.** The matrix travels with the design note to the security review and becomes the checklist for the three-cloud diagnosis lab, where the same boundaries are compared across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.

beats.recap: Every boundary gets a row with capture, location and status, and unknown rows stay unknown until a dated source or test closes them.

extensionCards.prompt: Which identity uses a Cloud KMS key when Databricks on Google Cloud encrypts with a customer-managed key?
extensionCards.answer: A service account that exists within the Databricks control-plane project, which must be allowed to use the key; with the manual option, the customer grants that access itself.
extensionCards.explanation: The account API describes the service account with access to a Google Cloud KMS key as existing within the Databricks control-plane project, and says that when manual is set Databricks will not use OAuth to grant it access, leaving the grant to the customer. Databricks' reference architecture separates managed services (notebooks, secrets and Databricks SQL query data in the control plane) from workspace storage (the two workspace storage buckets and the compute VMs' persistent disks), and its template applies the storage key to classic workspaces only. Tier and region requirements are unknown until verified.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It adds a service account owned by a Databricks project, and its key grant becomes a separate evidence row in the key's own IAM policy.

extensionCards.prompt: What can refuse a Cloud Storage request that IAM would allow, when a VPC Service Controls perimeter surrounds the bucket's project?
extensionCards.answer: The service perimeter itself: resources inside it exchange data freely, but a request whose source is inside and whose target is outside is blocked, whatever IAM says.
extensionCards.explanation: Google's Access Context Manager API describes a service perimeter as a set of resources that import and export data freely among themselves but not outside it, and a project can belong to only one regular perimeter. That makes it a third refusal layer beside IAM and organization policy, recognised by its own error. The Databricks SDK's endpoint rule model mentions all Google APIs that support VPC Service Controls, which shows the concept appears in the API; whether and how Databricks on Google Cloud supports perimeters is unknown until verified.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: A perimeter refusal looks like an access problem but no IAM grant fixes it, so diagnoses must recognise the layer by its error.

extensionCards.prompt: How can Cinderline ask Google which policy granted or withheld storage.objects.get for the credential's service account?
extensionCards.answer: Run Policy Troubleshooter for that principal, permission and bucket; it lists the IAM policies evaluated, including those inherited from the project, folder and organization.
extensionCards.explanation: Policy Troubleshooter takes the principal as input and returns the policies it evaluated, annotated with how each contributed, including inherited ones. Cloud Storage's testIamPermissions only reports the caller's own permissions, so it cannot speak for a Databricks-managed account. The troubleshooter's output is the evidence row: which binding allowed the permission, or that none did, recorded with the date and the exact principal, permission and resource checked.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It turns 'the grant looks right' into a recorded explanation for the exact principal, permission and resource in question.

extensionCards.prompt: Why might a Google Cloud storage credential's service account need Pub/Sub permissions as well as bucket roles?
extensionCards.answer: For file events on an external location: Databricks' guide grants that account a custom Pub/Sub role with storage.buckets.update, and gives the project's Cloud Storage service account the Pub/Sub publisher role.
extensionCards.explanation: Databricks' Unity Catalog guide for Google Cloud defines a custom role with Pub/Sub topic and subscription permissions and storage.buckets.update, grants it to the storage credential's service account at project level, and grants roles/pubsub.publisher to the project's Cloud Storage service account so bucket notifications can be published. These grants are project-wide, broader than the bucket binding, so they belong in the security review; the exact permission set must be read from the current guide.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It shows a storage credential can need project-level grants beyond the bucket, which a least-privilege review must see and justify.

recap.title: Projects, service accounts and two planes, each boundary with evidence
recap.markdown: **Cinderline's organization, folders and projects on one side; the Databricks account, control plane and serverless compute on the other.** A classic workspace names a project for its VMs and buckets and a VPC with one regional subnet, an outbound path and network-wide firewall rules; a serverless workspace names none of them. Every service account is read from its email's owning project, and a storage credential is a Databricks-managed service account that only bucket bindings make useful. Back-end PSC is two registered endpoints plus private DNS, and private access settings decide who reaches the workspace. A refusal names its layer; a timeout names none, so each gets its own ordered diagnosis. **Transfer challenge:** redraw the evidence matrix for a second region, mark which rows change, and keep every serverless connectivity cell unknown until a dated source settles it.

appliedTask.title: Move the nightly job to serverless and keep the evidence honest
appliedTask.prompt: Cinderline moves the nightly job from a classic cluster that reads gs://cl-quality-raw with its own google_service_account to a serverless SQL warehouse in cinderline-gcp-sls. The job also needs Ardent's bucket gs://ardent-parts-feed and a lookup in Cloud SQL on a private address in cl-vpc-dbx. List, in order, what must exist on the Google Cloud side and the Databricks side for each source, which responsibilities the move removes from Cinderline's projects, and what you would mark unknown before the design review.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: Google Cloud side: bindings on gs://cl-quality-raw for cred_quality's service account email, made by the data platform team, with the cluster account's binding removed once nothing else uses it; the same binding on gs://ardent-parts-feed, made by Ardent's administrator. Databricks side: storage credential cred_quality, external locations for both paths, READ FILES and SELECT for the job's run-as principal through its group, and the warehouse in the serverless workspace. Removed from Cinderline's projects: the cluster's VMs, their subnet addresses and relay traffic, and the cluster account's role in this path. Unknown until verified: serverless private access to the Cloud SQL lookup, which stays on a classic job meanwhile; whether Ardent's organization admits the binding; and the region and release status of serverless compute for Cinderline's account.
appliedTask.reasoning: The answer follows each source from principal through catalog to credential and binding, names who owns each grant, removes only what serverless actually removes, and turns every unsettled capability into an owned verification item instead of a promise.
